turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, Mr. Brennan, have a seat. What has you in today?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I've come about the type 2 diabetes. I've had it eight years... no, it'll be eleven years this autumn. The sugars have been up, and I thought I should not leave it.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Tell me how you've been in yourself, in your own words.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I've been tired, Doctor, more than usual. And thirsty. I'm drinking water all the day.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired and thirsty. Let me think — that pairing often goes with the sugar running high, though it can be other things. How long has the tiredness been with you?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, a few weeks, I would say. Since after the bank holiday. I couldn't put a date on the first day, I'm afraid.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's all right, we don't need the exact morning. And the thirst, same stretch of time?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor, the same. I'm up in the night to pass water as well, um, two or three times.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Passing water more at night. Any pain with that, or is it just the volume?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain, Doctor. Just that I'm going more.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. Now the home readings — what sort of figures are you seeing before breakfast?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): They're one-eighty-something, fasting. Sometimes I look and it's one-eighty-two, or one-eighty-seven, I don't write them down properly, I'm sorry.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): One-eighty-something is a bit loose for the chart. After your dinner, any number you trust?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Last night it was two-forty... no, I beg your pardon, it was two hundred and ten. I had misread the meter.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two hundred and ten after dinner, then. We'll stick with that. And these higher readings, still just those few weeks?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Before that they were nearer the target, or so I thought. My father had the sugar as well, in his later years.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you on for the type 2 at the moment?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The metformin, Doctor. Five hundred milligrams... no, sorry, they changed me to the thousand milligram tablets, one in the morning and one with the evening meal.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): A thousand milligrams twice a day, by mouth, with food. Anything else in tablet form?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. Just that, and the insulin.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): The insulin — talk me through it.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the Novorapid... no, I always say that wrong. It's the Lantus, the long-acting one. Eighteen units... forgive me, twenty-two units, every morning.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hmm. The nurse who checked you in has twenty-eight units of Lantus written on the sheet from what you told her. Twenty-two from you now, twenty-eight on her note.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm afraid the nurse has it wrong, Doctor. I draw up twenty-two. I have done since the spring.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I can't honestly put a dose in the record until we look at the pen together. Do you take it every morning?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Not every morning, I have to confess. On the days I'm in the office I sometimes leave the pen at home, and then I miss it.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many mornings in a week would that be?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Two or three, Doctor. I am sorry. I know that's not what was asked of me.

[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think out loud. If the long-acting insulin is missed two or three mornings, a fasting reading drifting to one-eighty-something would fit. It might also be that twenty-two units is simply light, even on the days you take it. I won't decide that today.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your wife rang the surgery yesterday. She said you were missing the insulin most days, and that your vision has been blurring when you read.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): With respect, Doctor, that isn't quite right. It is not most days, only the work mornings. And my sight is grand. She worries, but I am not blurring.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): So you and she don't agree on the eyes, and I'll leave that open. Any pain in the eyes, or floaters?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. Neither.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): When were you last at the retinal screening?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I am not certain. It was last autumn, I believe, or it may have been the spring before. I cannot be sure of the month.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll see if the record has a date. Feet now — any numbness, sores, or pain?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): A tingling in the toes at night, for months maybe. No sores, and no real pain. I do look, as I was told.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look now, if you'll slip the shoes off. Skin is intact on both feet, no breaks. The pulses are present. The monofilament is duller on the left big toe than the right.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I had noticed the left one feels different, yes.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any low sugars, the shakes, sweating, confusion?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor, I haven't had a hypo that I can recall.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, breathlessness, any change in the bowels?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): None of those, thank God.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines, or anything else?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I know of, Doctor.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, and what are you doing for work these days?

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. I work in the accounts office in town, five days, though some weeks I am in only three. There was a move of the filing room last month, which is why the pen gets left on the hall table, but that is neither here nor there.

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): It is actually quite here, the pen on the hall table. Blood pressure today is one thirty-six over eighty-four, and the pulse is seventy-four. My working impression is the diabetes is running high, most likely from the missed morning doses, though an under-dose is still possible, and I am not signing off on any eye problem while you and your wife differ.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): That seems fair, Doctor.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll send bloods for an HbA1c and the kidney function, and please bring the Lantus pen next time so we can settle the dose. Keep a spare pen at the office so the work mornings aren't missed, and check the feet each evening. I'll see you in four weeks. If a sore shows on the foot or the sight does change, come back before that, and if we cannot find a retinal screening within the year I'll refer you on.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

omissions.text: Fasting home glucose readings were reported as about 182-187 mg/dL before breakfast.
Metformin was specified to be taken with food: 1000 mg by mouth, one in the morning and one with the evening meal.
Lantus dose is not just missing but unresolved: patient states 22 units every morning and says the nurse's 28-unit note is wrong; doctor would not enter a dose until checking the pen.
Insulin adherence detail: the patient does not take Lantus every morning and misses it on two or three mornings per week, specifically on office/work days when he leaves the pen at home.

The patient denied blurred vision, stating 'my sight is grand' and 'I am not blurring'; the recorded fact incorrectly lists blurred vision as present rather than denied/disputed from the wife's report.
The patient denied numbness in the feet when asked about 'numbness, sores, or pain'.
Doctor noted uncertainty and specifically did not confirm any eye problem because the patient and his wife disagreed.
